shortlist.raw_text: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, enabling bidirectional context modeling and parallel token refinement. Recent studies have applied reinforcement learning (RL) to DLMs and improved their reasoning performance. However, the iterative denoising process makes credit assignment more challenging, as final outcome rewards provide limited information about how different tokens contribute to the final output. In this paper, we propose Denoising Token Credit Assignment (DTCA), a framework for token-level credit assignment in reinforcement learning for diffusion language models. DTCA estimates token contributions by measuring the improvement in prediction confidence of remaining masked positions after token commitment and groups these signals according to part-of-speech (POS) categories. These contribution weights are used to select informative denoising timesteps and assign token-level learning signals during RL training. DTCA further calibrates these learning signals according to token-level entropy changes induced by policy updates. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct show that DTCA consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance across different generation budgets, with gains of up to 9.0 points on MATH500 and 5.3 points on GSM8K over the base model.

shortlist.raw_text: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

shortlist.raw_text: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all. Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes. “There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.” The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says. Download the report This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

Title: The future of the firm

Text:
How AI might enter the org chart—beneath, beside, and between us.

Article text (excerpt):
How AI might enter the org chart—beneath, beside, and between us.
Authors’ note: This is the second essay in our series on the next economy, part of a new platform to host independent voices exploring an AGI future. It reflects our views, not those of OpenAI or our colleagues.
The two of us were twenty-four when we started managing our own teams here at OpenAI. That is less impressive once you meet our teams.
We’re supposed to be grunts. At twenty-four, you’re at the bottom of the corporate ladder. You take the meeting notes and write a few memos. After years of drudgerous work, you are (hopefully) granted a broader remit.
Our path—and the path of many young people today—is looking different. We enter the workforce already with “employees” at our behest. These deputies work day and night, weekends and holidays. They are great at the grunt work. We even have math olympiad gold medalists on staff to advise us. Our new reports still make their share of mistakes. But they are getting better, learning our needs, and we are learning how to manage them.
Neither of us climbed the corporate ladder. Management has instead come down to our rung. This essay is about our promotion, and the other ways firms might reorganize as we enter the intelligence age.
When AI enters the firm, where does it go? We present three illustrative scenarios:
Beneath us. Everyone keeps their seat, and a new basement of AI labor grows underneath. We all become managers. First we get assistants, then chiefs of staff, and eventually entire miniature firms reporting up to each of us. Every person gets a promotion.
Beside us. AI joins the org chart alongside people as a colleague of sorts, working directly for existing human managers and executives. It starts out by taking up this task and that role. In time, it performs broader functions, reporting higher up the flagpole.
Between us. The most unintuitive case: humans above and humans below, with AI in between. It coordinates and monitors work, enforcing an executive’s vision while recognizing unique contributions from enterprising workers.
None of these scenarios will play out exactly as we describe, but we think aspects of all three will come true. All three are already happening in subtle ways.
Our focus here isn’t total automation but a transitioning economy. We are interested in what chimeric firms will look like as AI improves and laces itself into existing organizations.
We believe the hybrid firm is conceptually important because productive adoption of AI isn’t instantaneous. When the models only do a subset of tasks, adoption may be easiest by ground-level employees familiar with the work. Once the models perform broad functions end-to-end, higher-ups can use them directly. In our view, more capable AI is more adoptable: firms must learn technologies, but labor learns the firm and can onboard itself.
We’ll dissect the three new classes of org chart, then examine what they mean for the future of red tape, worker agency, firm size, and pay disparity.
Our first scenario seems least disruptive. Here, people stay in the same seats with the same reporting lines, ostensibly doing the same jobs as before. The human org chart looks unchanged between today and this future.
The difference is below us. Beneath each individual contributor, a new AI labor force reports up to each of us. Our org chart gets a basement, and we all become managers.
At first, this basement is unfinished. We start with one or two agents apiece, less as seasoned employees, more as eager interns we must supervise and readily forgive. Our expectations are low: send an email here, draft a memo there, reply to Slack messages everywhere. Like junior human employees, they begin with little autonomy and trust.
But as models improve, our agents take on more tasks with less supervision. They coordinate with each other. There might be manager AIs and grunt AIs, accountants and lawyers, all working together at your behest. Far from handholding an intern, your operation eventually looks like a small firm in its own right, with its own org chart and you as its board of directors.
Jace still does the accounting at his firm, but he’s no longer clicking around the spreadsheets. His agent underlings do that. Jace’s job is more like his manager’s from a few years ago. His manager, in turn, now has an even bigger remit.
Jace’s day-to-day has completely changed, now focused on communication, coordination, and creativity. He works less and feels more challenged. His work life has more variance, and he distinguishes himself with leadership skills and a vision he couldn’t showcase before.
The accounting team hasn’t shrunk because the rest of the company has grown more productive too and demands more accounting than ever before. The agents can’t yet do everything his team does. The execs wouldn’t know the first thing about assembling financial data and need his domain expertise to use the agents effectively.
Notice how this scenario doesn’t imply layoffs. Here we adopt AI without automating ourselves. We instead automate our past selves , and we move up in the hierarchy. AI takes on more and more of what we used to do. Our jobs remain because there is more to manage, and we gain responsibility for a greater sum of output.
Jobs aren’t static ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Suppose that AI can do ninety percent of what you did before. You might conclude you’re left with only ten percent of the work. The other possibility is that you’re still doing a full job, just a different one—now focused on an objective ten times larger. That is the classic gift of technology: productivity rises, ambition rises to meet it, and wages can rise ⁠ (opens in a new window) with the ambition.
This all depends on whether we still add value ⁠ (opens in a new window) to production. This essay focuses on the coming years where automation isn’t universally capable or adopted. Even if AI could do it all, we might still value something more because a person made it, or insist that a person have the final say.
It also depends on our appetite. If, as consumers, we don’t care for ten times more output, the equilibrium will shift toward fewer workers or fewer hours worked. Historically, increases in output have not satiated us. We have a lot more ⁠ (opens in a new window) but work only a little less ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Should our appetite continue to grow as output multiplies—and we remain additive to production—we will choose to keep trading our labor for more consumption. If instead production becomes so abundant that we are satiated, we might volunteer a smaller labor force.
There are more objections we discuss later (e.g. whether we’ll have a larger number of smaller firms). We still think this scenario is important because adoption has to start somewhere. Firms need a way to stably evolve from their current org structures. Bolstering the work of existing employees may be an easier first step than wholesale restructuring. We see this in action today: one worker after another delegating to AI, without an organizational revolution so far.
This scenario relies on the front line hiring first. Ground-level workers—not managers and executives—lead on AI adoption. That appears likely, so long as the person who best gets AI to do the work is the person who used to do it themselves.
Models can already automate many data science tasks, but a department head unfamiliar with the methods and minutiae will struggle to leverage the tools. Until AI becomes proactive enough to tell you what you don’t know (see our next scenario), it will probably work best for those already familiar with how the work is done.
The biggest change in this scenario is for entry-level workers. There would no longer be a lowest rung, at least not for humans. When we hire young people, it won’t be to place them at the drudgerous bottom of the firm. Those positions will be filled by something that doesn’t mind.
With that, we lose some traditional routes to educate young workers: the apprenticeship ⁠ (opens in a new window) , the learning-by-grunt-work, the earning of stripes. These are genuine costs, but we mostly see this as a privilege. The greenest hire with a good idea has resources to experiment. The oldest excuse in the building, we just don’t have the manpower , is dying. A junior employee with a great video game in her head and no path to the headcount can now simply build it.
In our view, this “promoting” scenario still has much for junior workers to learn—judgment, taste, the muscles of management and creative vision. We will be incentivized to cultivate these skills because they show up in our work product. We will still learn by doing ⁠ (opens in a new window) , but at a higher level of scope. Firm elders remain incentivized to help us as responsible stewards (with equity stakes in our success). The opportunity here is a more stimulating role for everyone at every rung. text:
Two 24-year-old OpenAI managers just proposed a new corporate org chart.

Instead of cutting jobs from above, AI enters at the very bottom beneath everyday workers.

Here is what that changes for your team.

The authors call it the basement scenario.

Your current reporting lines stay the same, but a layer of AI labor grows under every employee.

Front-line workers lead the adoption because they already know how the work gets done.

At first, the basement starts small:
• One or two agents draft emails and reply to Slack messages
• Advanced models coordinate with each other to handle complex tasks
• Human workers shift entirely to coordination and strategy

That turns individual contributors into personal boards of directors.

Take an accountant named Jace in the essay.

He stops clicking spreadsheets while his agent underlings process the data, letting his firm handle far more output.

That reveals the core idea: if AI automates 90 percent of your old tasks, you do not work 10 percent of a job.

You run a role with an objective 10 times larger.

The biggest casualty is the traditional entry-level position.

The lowest rung of corporate drudgery disappears, along with classic grunt-work apprenticeships.

My read: the early AI transition will not look like executive-led layoffs.

It will look like entry-level hires managing software teams on day one.

The limit is real: this essay reflects the opinions of two internal managers, not a verified industry study.

Are you ready to manage a team on your first day at work?

Source: OpenAI
